mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Monday, November 2, 2026. Anthropic has warned in a recent regulatory filing that it is nearing the threshold of recursive self-improvement, or RSI. This concept describes a point where an AI model becomes sufficiently capable to train and upgrade itself, potentially leading to a rapid, uncontrollable acceleration in development. While Anthropic emphasized that no current model has reached this stage and noted its intention to keep humans in the research and development process, the company stated that it has already observed leaps in model capabilities that its internal teams did not initially recognize. Anthropic cautioned that if its models begin to advance faster than safety and alignment measures can be developed, it may not identify significant accelerations until after they have occurred. This disclosure highlights the ongoing tension between the pursuit of advanced AI productivity and the risks of systems moving beyond human oversight. For Anthropic, managing RSI is a core component of its Responsible Scaling Policy, which is intended to mitigate risks as the company’s models grow in coding, math, and cybersecurity proficiency. In the infrastructure sector, OpenAI has announced the Grid Protectors Program to manage the energy demands of its future compute campuses. The company plans to work with utilities and regulators to implement flexible power usage, allowing its facilities to reduce electricity demand during periods of high grid strain, such as extreme heat or cold. OpenAI stated that it intends to cover the full costs of necessary infrastructure upgrades for its projects, using its campus in Effingham County, Georgia, as a pilot for this model. The company suggests that by adjusting its power consumption, it can help stabilize the grid for local households and businesses. This initiative responds to the massive growth in data center capacity, which is projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030, and aims to ensure that compute facilities act as supportive grid citizens rather than adding to peak demand stress. Separately, the web hosting company Squarespace is laying off approximately 19% of its workforce, impacting around 300 employees. The company stated the restructuring is intended to sharpen its operational focus. This move occurs amidst a shifting landscape for website builders, which are increasingly integrating generative AI to allow users to create front-end designs through simple prompts. The broader industry has seen rapid changes, including acquisitions and high-value funding rounds for startups focused on AI-native website creation, such as the startup Lovable, which recently raised a $400 million Series C round. Squarespace, which returned to private ownership in 2024, has been integrating tools like Blueprint and the upcoming platform Forma to remain competitive in an environment where generative AI is reducing the effort required to build functional websites. In research and application, several updates highlight the evolving economics and performance of agentic AI. OpenAI introduced LifeVal, a new evaluation framework designed to measure how well AI models assist with everyday tasks—such as caregiving, household administration, and personal finance—using data from time-use surveys to track progress toward becoming a practical personal assistant. Meanwhile, reporting on enterprise analytics indicates that while agentic AI is becoming more capable, over half of the insights generated by current agents fail to lead to actionable business improvements, often due to a lack of necessary business context or fragmented data. To address the rising costs of these agentic workflows, AWS has released guidance on using knowledge distillation. This technique involves training a smaller, more cost-effective student model to replicate the performance of a larger, more powerful teacher model, helping developers reduce the high expenses associated with running complex, multi-step agentic loops. Similarly, industry experts are increasingly suggesting that organizations should move away from measuring AI performance solely by token consumption. Instead, they recommend tracking the cost per completed project, such as the number of merged software pull requests, to better identify the actual value generated by AI-assisted development.
